accuracy.evidence: Checked against the national curriculum in England, English Appendix 2 Year 6 (hyphens to avoid ambiguity, with man eating shark v man-eating shark and recover v re-cover) and the Years 5–6 spelling appendix (hyphens join a prefix to a root word, especially when the vowels at the end of the prefix and start of the root are the same: co-ordinate, re-enter, co-operate, co-own), and against New Hart's Rules ch. 4 hyphenation (compound modifiers hyphenated before but not after the noun; no hyphen after an -ly adverb; re-cover/recover, re-sign/resign, re-count/recount distinguished by the hyphen). Every lab word was checked by hand: re-enter, co-own and re-elect have doubled vowels; rebuild, rearrange (e then a) and misspell (doubled consonant) are solid; twenty-odd means about twenty. The -ly rule is stated for adverbs only, so it stays true for adjectives like friendly.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real hyphen slips: hyphenating every prefix (re-build in SLIP 2, m8), running a doubled vowel together (reenter in SLIP 1, JOIN 'Just join' feedback), treating any two vowels as a clash (re + arrange prediction and JOIN 4 feedback 'e and a are different vowels'), thinking a doubled consonant needs a hyphen (misspell), hyphenating a compound after the noun (SPOT 2 and 5, prediction 4, challenge q4), a hyphen after an -ly adverb (SPOT 3, SLIP 3, m4), a partial hyphen in a three-word compound (challenge q6), and treating recover and re-cover as the same word (prediction 1, PAIR feedback, m3, m9).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghyph is built on where a hyphen sits in a word or phrase: a sentence gap filled with recover or re-cover by meaning, a prefix tile and root tile with the two meeting letters named before the learner chooses join or hyphen, a phrase whose gaps can each take a hyphen so the learner moves it to match a stated meaning (or leaves it out), a before-or-after-the-noun hyphen check, and a tap-the-wrong-word slip finder. flagmarks (lesson 454) has a single man-eating step among five marks and flagunpre (776) teaches the meaning of un-; neither teaches prefix hyphen rules or hyphen position. lab_distinct gate under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The rules come out of the feedback, not a list: choosing recover for the torn sofa returns 'This one needs cover it again, so it is re-cover'; Just join for re + enter returns 'Joined it reads reenter, which is hard to read'; Add a hyphen for re + arrange says 'e and a are different vowels, so join'; putting the hyphen in a-man says the wrong pair is joined; No hyphen for 'a well known author' says it comes before the noun author, so join it.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the task disproves, and the step text no longer gives the answer away: 'yes, the hyphen is just style' (PAIR shows recover and re-cover fit different sentences), 'yes, two vowels meet' for re + arrange (JOIN 4 is Just join), 'the shark is eating people' for an unhyphenated man eating shark (PIC 2 needs No hyphen for a man eating shark meat), and 'yes, well-known always has one' (SPOT 2 is No hyphen). A.reveal names the locked-in pick when each task ends.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with twelve wrong-answer messages naming the slip: recover means get well, a prefix is never a word on its own, e meets h so just join reheat, e and a are different vowels, no hyphen makes a man eat shark, the hyphen must join man and eating, after the noun leave out the hyphen, before the noun it needs one, -ly adverbs never take a hyphen, never split the -ly ending, three words need hyphens, and all three words go together in eleven-year-old.

readability.evidence: learn/readability.py: kid FK grade 3.0 (family limit 5.0), adult 7.6 (limit 10.0) after the adult text was split into shorter sentences (first draft scored 12.6). Kid paragraphs use one example each (rebuild, Gran will recover, re-enter, a well-known author). Canvas sentences are short and the feedback is one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs cover what a hyphen does, recover v re-cover, the same-vowel rule with a counter-example (rearrange), and before-v-after the noun. Adult text gives the Year 6 Appendix 2 and spelling-appendix statements, the solid-by-default rule, five named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and the explanation is under 12% similar to every other lesson, including 454 grammar terms and 776 the prefix un-.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark for all six steps and a wrong-answer state on each task (recover picked for the sofa, Just join for re + enter, hyphen in a-man, No hyphen for a well known author, Please tapped as the slip). The phrase row in step 3 first clipped 'a' and 'shark' at 360 px; the font now shrinks until the words and gaps fit. Answer tiles are at least 56 px tall. Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a button under the canvas: recover / re-cover (labelled 'Use re-cover'), the joined and hyphened word ('Add a hyphen: re-enter'), one button per possible hyphen position plus No hyphen ('Hyphen between man and eating'), Needs a hyphen / No hyphen, and one button per word in the slip sentence ('reenter is wrong'). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, warnings switch to #fda4af on dark, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
